Chapter 4. Paññā (wisdom)

“Paññā lokasmi pajjoto”: Wisdom is the light in the world. (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.80)

Paññā (wisdom) means seeing things as they really are. Without it, the other nine cannot do their work well. The Buddha said that wisdom is the light in the world. A lamp in a dark room shows what is there. Wisdom is like that lamp.

Sumedha’s picture. Sumedha thought of a monk1 on his morning walk for food. The monk goes to every house, big or small, rich or poor. He passes none of them by. So he gets enough to eat. Sumedha said: go to wise people like that, everywhere and always, and ask them questions. That is how wisdom grows.

the monk on his round goes to every house and passes none by so wisdom grows by asking every wise person, everywhere and always

a big house a middle house a small house “Yathāpi bhikkhu bhikkhanto, hīnamukkaṭṭhamajjhime; kulāni na vivajjento, evaṃ labhati yāpanaṃ”: Like a monk on his round for food, who passes by no family, low, high or in between, and so gets enough to live on. (Buddhavaṃsa 2)

The story of the boy Mahosadha. Once the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) was born as a boy named Mahosadha. When he was seven years old he was already so wise that people came to him with their quarrels. Here is one of them.

A woman went to a pond to wash, and laid her baby down on the bank. A yakkhinī (a wicked spirit) saw the baby and wanted to eat it. She came in the shape of a woman and offered to hold the baby while the mother washed. Then she ran off with it. The mother ran after her and caught her. Each of them said: this is my child.

They came to Mahosadha. He listened. Then he drew a line on the ground and laid the baby across it. He told the yakkhinī (the wicked spirit) to take the baby’s hands and the mother to take its feet, and he said: pull. Whoever pulls the baby over the line can have it.

They pulled. The baby cried out in pain. The mother could not bear to hurt her child. She let go, and stood there weeping. The yakkhinī (the wicked spirit) held on and kept pulling.

Mahosadha asked the people: whose heart is soft for a child, the mother’s or a stranger’s? They said: the mother’s. He said: then this one is the mother. He gave her the baby. And he showed everyone that the other was a yakkhinī (a wicked spirit): her eyes were red and did not blink, and she had no shadow. He made her promise to keep the five rules, and sent her away.

Mahosadha was not at the pond. He did not see what happened there. But he knew what a mother’s love is like, and he knew how to make it show itself. That is paññā (wisdom): seeing what is really so.

Anna learns. Anna cannot see inside her mind with her eyes. But she can learn what is there. Seeing is one thing. Hearing is another. Liking is another. Anger is another. Learning to tell them apart is the beginning of paññā (wisdom). It comes from listening and asking, just as Sumedha said.

No one inside. Paññā (wisdom) is not a person either. It is a good quality that comes up with a moment of mind, sees, and goes. The clearest thing it sees is this: there is no self in here. There are only moments, coming and going. Anna says: sabbe dhammā anattā (all things are not self).

HARD WORDS IN THIS CHAPTER 1. monk: a man who has left home to follow the Buddha's rule of life

Chapter 5. Viriya (energy)

“Vāyametheva puriso, na nibbindeyya paṇḍito”: A person should keep on striving. A wise person does not give up. (Jātaka 539) Viriya (energy1) means effort. It is the strength in the mind that keeps going, and does not give up, and does not get lazy. The Buddha said that by energy a person gets past suffering2. Sumedha’s picture. Sumedha thought of a lion. Whether the lion sits, or stands, or walks, it is never slack. Its mind is always awake. Sumedha said: keep up firm energy like the lion, in every life.

the lion is never slack; its mind is always awake viriya (energy) in every life, like the lion

sitting standing walking “Yathāpi sīho migarājā, nisajjaṭṭhānacaṅkame; alīnavīriyo hoti, paggahitamano sadā”: Like the lion, king of beasts: sitting, standing or walking, it is never slack in energy, and its mind is always alert. (Buddhavaṃsa 2)

The story of Prince Mahājanaka. Once the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) was a prince named Mahājanaka. His father had been a king, but his uncle took the kingdom, and the prince grew up far away with his mother. When he was grown, he wanted to win the kingdom back. So he got on a ship with goods to sell, to earn money for it.

In the middle of the ocean the ship broke apart. The people on it screamed and wept. Mahājanaka did not scream. He ate until he was full, so that he would have strength. He rubbed oil on his body, so that the water would not make him cold. Then he climbed the mast and jumped as far out as he could, away from the sinking ship and the hungry fish. And he began to swim.

He swam all day. He swam all night. He swam for seven days. There was no land anywhere.

A goddess of the sea named Maṇimekhalā saw him. She asked him who he was, swimming in the middle of the ocean with no shore in sight, and what the use of it was. She said he would die before he reached land.

Mahājanaka answered that a person should do what a person can do. Someone who makes an effort has nothing to be sorry for, even if he fails. And he said: I will go on striving, as far as I can and as hard as I can.

The goddess was pleased. She lifted him out of the water and carried him through the air to his own country. She laid him down, asleep, in a mango grove. In the end he became king there.

Energy for good and energy for bad. Energy is in bad moments too. A person can work very hard to grab something he wants, or to get back at someone. That is not the perfection3. The perfection of viriya (energy) is effort for kusala (good).

Anna keeps going. Anna is tidying her room. She is tired. She wants to stop. She puts away one more thing. Then one more. That is viriya (energy). The prince swam for seven days. Anna puts away one more thing. Both are the same kind of thing.

No one inside. Who swam? Mahājanaka, the story says. But the arm moves because a moment of mind with viriya (energy) in it moves the arm. Then that moment is gone. The next moment has to have energy too, or the arm stops. Nobody inside pushes. There is energy, moment after moment, and each moment helps the next one to come.

HARD WORDS IN THIS CHAPTER 1. energy: effort; the strength that keeps on going 3. perfection: a good quality made as full and strong as it can be 2. suffering: pain and trouble; anything that cannot give lasting happiness

Chapter 6. Khanti (patience)

“Yadihaṃ tassa pakuppeyyaṃ, tato hīnataro bhave; sīlañca me pabhijjeyya, viññū ca garaheyyu maṃ”: If I were angry with him, I would be lower than he is. My good conduct would break, and the wise would blame me. (Cariyāpiṭaka 2.5) Khanti (patience) means putting up with things without getting angry. Hot weather. Cold weather. A long wait. A mosquito. Someone being unkind. The Buddha said that patience is the highest tapa (burning away). It burns away the dirt in the mind. Sumedha’s picture. Sumedha thought of the earth. People throw clean things on the earth, and dirty things too. The earth bears them all. It is never angry. Sumedha said: bear honour and insult from everyone, like the earth.

khanti (patience) bears honour and insult like the earth

clean things dirty things the earth bears them all and is never angry “Yathāpi pathavī nāma, sucimpi asucimpi ca; sabbaṃ sahati nikkhepaṃ, na karoti paṭighaṃ tayā”: Like the earth, which bears everything thrown on it, clean or unclean, and is not angry about it. (Buddhavaṃsa 2)

The story of the buffalo and the monkey. Once the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) was born as a great buffalo. He was big and strong, with wide horns. He lived in the forest, and he had a favourite place under a tree, where he stood and where he slept.

A monkey lived in that tree. The monkey was rude and naughty. He jumped on the buffalo’s back. He sat on his shoulder, and on his forehead, and even between his horns. He pulled his ears and swung on his horns. He made a mess all over him. Not once. Day after day.

A yakkha (a spirit) who lived in the tree saw it all. He said to the buffalo: why put up with this? Kill him. One push with the horns, one stamp with a foot, and he is gone.

The buffalo answered: this monkey is small and weak and silly. If I were angry with him, I would be lower than he is. My sīla (good conduct) would break, and wise people would blame me. It is better to be laughed at and keep a clean mind than to hurt another to save my own life. And he said: if I put up with him, I will get what I am hoping for. What he was hoping for was to become a Buddha.

So the buffalo stood still. Later the monkey tried the same tricks on another buffalo, a fierce one, and that buffalo killed him. But the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) never hurt him.

Anna and the mosquito. It is a hot night. A mosquito whines by Anna’s ear. She wants to shout. She does not. She waves it away gently. That is khanti (patience). It is small, as the buffalo’s patience was big.

No one inside. When anger comes, it feels like “I am angry”. But anger is dosa (anger), a visitor, like wanting. It comes up with one moment of mind, and it goes. The moment that was angry is already gone. There is nobody who has to stay angry. When that is seen, patience comes more easily. Anna says: sabbe dhammā anattā (all things are not self).

Chapter 7. Sacca (truthfulness)

“Santi pakkhā apatanā, santi pādā avañcanā; mātāpitā ca nikkhantā, jātaveda paṭikkama”: I have wings, but they cannot fly. I have feet, but they cannot walk. My mother and father have gone away. Fire, go back! (Jātaka 35) Sacca (truthfulness1) means telling the truth and keeping one’s word. The Buddha said that truth is the sweetest of all tastes. The old books say that in some lives the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) broke other rules, but he never once told a lie. Sumedha’s picture. Sumedha thought of the morning star. In every season, in rain or in sun, the morning star keeps to its path across the sky. It never strays from it. Sumedha said: never stray from the path of truth.

the morning star rain sun

in every season it keeps to its path and never strays sacca (truthfulness) keeps to the path of truth like that “Yathāpi osadhī nāma, tulābhūtā sadevake; samaye utuvasse vā, na vokkamati vīthito”: Like the morning star, steady for the whole world: in any season, in any weather, it never leaves its path. (Buddhavaṃsa 2)

The story of the little quail. Once the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) was born as a baby quail. He lay in a nest on the ground. He was tiny. His wings had no feathers yet, so he could not fly. His legs were weak, so he could not walk. His mother and father fed him from their beaks.

One hot day a fire started in the forest. It came roaring and crackling, nearer and nearer. All the birds flew away. The quail’s mother and father were afraid. They flew away too, and left the baby in the nest.

The little quail thought: I have wings, but I cannot fly. I have feet, but I cannot run. My mother and father have gone. What can I do?

Then he thought: there is truth in the world. There is goodness. The Buddhas of long ago had it. By that truth I will make an act of truth.

And he said: I have wings, but they cannot fly. I have feet, but they cannot walk. My mother and father have gone away. Fire, go back! The fire stopped. It turned back, as if it had run into water. It went out all round the nest. The old books say that nothing has burnt on that spot ever since, and nothing will, for the whole age of the world.

That is called saccakiriyā (an act of truth). When someone says a thing that is really true about himself, and calls on that truth, the truth has power. The quail had never told a lie, and he had never harmed anything.

Anna and the cup. Anna knocks a cup off the table. It breaks. Nobody saw. She could say she does not know how it happened. She says: I did it. That is sacca (truthfulness). It is hard for a moment. Then it is over, and the mind is clean.

No one inside. The deepest truth is the truth about the mind. There was seeing. There was a thought. There was fear. There was a true word. Each one came and went. No Anna inside did them all. Being truthful about that, moment by moment, is the beginning of the wisdom the Buddha taught.

HARD WORDS IN THIS CHAPTER 1. truthfulness: always telling the truth and keeping to it

Chapter 8. Adhiṭṭhāna (determination)

“Adhiṭṭhānena me samo natthi, esā me adhiṭṭhānapāramī”: In determination there was no one equal to me. This was my perfection of determination. (Cariyāpiṭaka 3.6)

Adhiṭṭhāna (determination1) means making up one’s mind to do good and not letting go of it, even when it is very hard, and even when it takes a very long time.

Sumedha’s picture. Sumedha thought of a mountain made of rock. The strongest wind blows. The mountain does not move. It stays in its own place. Sumedha said: be like that mountain in determination, always.

the strongest wind

the mountain of rock does not move; it stays in its own place adhiṭṭhāna (determination) is like the mountain “Yathāpi pabbato selo, acalo suppatiṭṭhito; na kampati bhusavātehi, sakaṭṭhāneva tiṭṭhati”: Like a mountain of rock, unmoving and well set: strong winds do not shake it, and it stays in its own place. (Buddhavaṃsa 2)

The story of Prince Temiya. Once the Bodhisatta (the Buddha-to-be) was born as a prince named Temiya. His father was the king of Kāsi. The king had waited a long time for a son, and he loved the baby very much.

When Temiya was one month old, the king held him on his lap while he judged four robbers. The king gave them terrible punishments. The baby heard it, and he was frightened. He remembered that long ago he had been a king himself, and that after that life he had gone to niraya (hell) because of the things he had done as king. He thought: I do not want to be king.

A deva (a heavenly being2) who lived in the royal umbrella had been his mother in a past life. She told him what to do: pretend to be a child who cannot walk, cannot hear and cannot speak. Then nobody will make him king.

So Temiya made up his mind. He lay still. He did not speak. He did not seem to hear. He did not walk.

His parents could not believe it. They tested him for sixteen years. They gave him no milk for a whole day: he did not cry. They gave him sweets and toys: he did not reach for them. They made loud noises: he did not jump. They let a big elephant come close: he did not run. They lit a fire near him: he did not move. Sixteen years. He never once let go of his plan.

At last the king gave up. He said: this boy brings bad luck. Take him to the forest and bury him.

The charioteer3 drove Temiya to the forest and began to dig a hole. Then Temiya thought: now is my time. He stretched his arms. He stretched his legs. He stood up. He was so strong that he lifted the chariot4 with one hand, as a boy lifts a toy. The charioteer was amazed. Temiya told him everything, and said that he would stay in the forest and live as a hermit5.

The king and the queen came to see him. When they found him well and happy, and heard him teach, they too gave up the palace and lived in the forest.

Wishing is not deciding. A wish is light. It blows away. Adhiṭṭhāna (determination) is heavy, like the mountain.

Anna makes up her mind. Anna decides to say a kind word to everyone in her class, every day, for a week. On the third day she is tired and grumpy. She says the kind word anyway. That is adhiṭṭhāna (determination).

No one inside. Sixteen years is a long time. But Temiya did not have one self that stayed the same for sixteen years. There was a moment of firm, good mind. Then another. Then another. Each one was helped by the one before it. That is how determination works: not one big self holding on, but good moments following good moments, like steps along a road. Anna says: sabbe dhammā anattā (all things are not self).
